summary: Expands destination-based remote triggered black hole filtering, a technique to mitigate denial-of-service attacks, by combining it with unicast Reverse Path Forwarding so traffic can also be filtered by source address. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network is flooded with traffic aimed at one customer, the usual response is to throw that traffic away at the edge of the network rather than carry it. This RFC describes how to do that with ordinary routing, and how to aim the same mechanism at the attacker instead of the victim.

questions: what is remote triggered black hole filtering
source based vs destination based filtering
subtitle: How a network operator can drop an attack at the edge of the network, and how the same trick can be aimed at the attacker's address instead.

tldr.problem: A denial-of-service attack floods a customer's address with more traffic than the links towards it can carry, starving out the legitimate traffic and hurting the rest of the network on the way.
tldr.mechanism: The operator announces a routing entry with BGP that points at a discard interface, so that the affected traffic is thrown away at the edge of the network instead of crossing it.
tldr.outcome: Destination-based black holing takes the target fully offline, so the RFC adds a source-based variant that uses unicast Reverse Path Forwarding to drop traffic from the attacker's address instead.

facts.label: Attacks that led to the tool
facts.value: February 2000 attacks on content hosting companies

today: RFC 5635 is an Informational memo published in August 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol: it describes how to configure BGP and unicast Reverse Path Forwarding on existing routers, and gives partial Cisco and Juniper configurations as examples.

sections.title: The Problem and the Black Hole Answer
sections.content:
A common denial-of-service attack aimed at a customer of a service provider sends more traffic to the target than will fit down the links from the providers to the victim. The attack traffic starves out legitimate traffic, and it often causes collateral damage or negative effects for other customers and for the network infrastructure as well. Instead of letting every destination on the network suffer, the customer may ask the provider to filter traffic destined for the target addresses, or the provider may decide to do so itself in order to preserve network availability.

One way to implement this filtering is to deploy access control lists on the edge of the network. That gives a lot of flexibility, but it runs into scalability problems, both in the number of entries in the filter and in the rate at which packets can be filtered. Most routers forward traffic far faster than they can filter it, and they hold far more forwarding table entries and routes than filter entries. Remote Triggered Black Hole (RTBH) filtering uses the forwarding performance of modern routers instead, so it can filter more entries at a higher rate than access control lists would allow.

With destination-based RTBH, however, the impact on the target is complete. The discard route is injected into the forwarding table for the target prefix, and all packets towards that destination, attack traffic and legitimate traffic alike, are dropped by the participating routers. The target is taken fully offline. The benefit is that collateral damage to other systems, to network availability at the customer location and to the ISP network is limited; the cost is that the target itself is hurt more, not less.

RFC 5635 expands on the technique described in RFC 3882 by showing how BGP can distribute discard routes based on the source addresses of unwanted traffic rather than on the destination. Coupling RTBH with unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) from RFC 3704 makes that possible. The document is in three parts: how to configure destination-based RTBH, how to do source-based RTBH, and then examples and a history of the technique.
sections.plainLanguage: Flooding one address with traffic hurts the whole network on the way to that address. The standard answer is to drop the traffic at the edge, but the usual version also cuts the victim off completely. This RFC shows how to aim the same trick at the attacker instead.

sections.title: Setting Up Destination-Based Black Holing
sections.content:
Some planning has to happen before any of this is deployed. The RFC lists the decisions: what the discard addresses will be, what the discard BGP communities will be, what the largest prefix that can be black-holed is, and what the smallest advertisement the provider will accept.

Step 1, choose the discard address scheme. An address is picked to become the discard address, often from 192.0.2.0/24 (TEST-NET) or from the private address space of RFC 1918. Several addresses let the operator configure several static routes, one for each incident, for example 192.0.2.1 for incident one and 192.0.2.2 for incident two. Where the router can count the drops, it can then give some telemetry on the volume of drops and on the state of an ongoing attack. A consistent address scheme makes operations easier.

Step 2, configure the discard route on each router. A route for the discard address is installed on the routers that form the edge or perimeter of the network, in all of them or in some subset such as the peering routers but not the customer routers. The destination of the route is set to the discard or null interface. Implementation experience shows the value of giving every ingress router the capability to drop traffic this way.

Step 3, configure the RTBH BGP policy on each router. A BGP policy is configured on every router holding the discard route so that routes announced with a chosen community have their next hop set to the discard address. The policy should be restrictive, so that only routes covering a defined number of host addresses are accepted. Typically only specific /32s are needed. Shorter prefix blocks may be required or desirable, for example when many attack targets sit inside one prefix, or when the mechanism is used to drop traffic bound for a whole network, but extreme caution is needed then, because of the collateral damage to other hosts inside those blocks. Full implementations use several communities, each for a different part of the provider's network and a different security incident.

Step 4, configure the safety egress prefix filters. There is always a chance that the triggering BGP update leaks out of the network, so egress prefix filters are strongly recommended. Deny all prefixes longer than the longest prefix expected to be announced, for example if the longest expected is /24 then deny /25 through /32, and deny all the communities used for triggering the filtering. Both are safety measures in case the NO_EXPORT community does not work as intended.

Step 5, configure the trigger router. The trigger router, workstation or other device should make it easy and quick to add and remove triggers. The BGP update should carry the NO_EXPORT community as a mandatory attribute, and an egress filter that keeps filtering prefixes out of the /8 to /24 range is recommended as a safety tool. The trigger router can be set up as an iBGP route reflector client that receives no prefixes from its BGP peer, which allows a low-cost router or workstation to do the job.

In use, the address that needs filtering is announced from the trigger router, tagged with the chosen RTBH community and with NO_EXPORT, and passed over iBGP. The receiving routers apply their BGP policy, set the next hop to the discard route, and end up with a forwarding entry pointing at the discard address. Traffic entering the network is then forwarded to the discard interface on all edge routers and dropped at the edge, which saves resources. The RFC describes three extensions: several discard addresses, so that the volume of discarded traffic can be monitored per incident; several trigger communities, so that different parts of the network can be switched on separately, with an example schema of XXX:600 for all routers, XXX:601 for peering routers only, XXX:602 for customers who peer BGP, XXX:603 for data centres and XXX:604 for all customers; and customer-triggered filtering, where the Autonomous System path rule is relaxed so that a customer can request it, in which case the operator must only accept announcements for prefixes the customer is authorised to advertise.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting this up takes five steps: pick the addresses that mean throw away, point a route at them on the edge routers, write the rule that matches the trigger, add filters so the trigger cannot escape, and set up a small machine that sends the trigger.

sections.title: Black Holing the Attacker Instead
sections.content:
Botnet attacks are often configured to follow DNS: the attacking machines are told to attack a host name and re-resolve it periodically. Attacks used to be aimed simply at an IP address, so renumbering the host to a new address was an effective mitigation, and that trick no longer works. This is what makes it desirable to black-hole based on the source address.

Combining RTBH filtering with uRPF does it. uRPF performs a route lookup on the source address of the packet and checks whether the ingress interface is a valid egress interface for that source, in strict mode, or whether any route to the source exists, in loose mode. If the check fails, the packet is typically dropped. In loose mode some vendors also verify that the destination route does not point at an invalid next hop, which allows source-based RTBH filtering to be deployed in networks that cannot implement strict mode. Before enabling uRPF in any mode, the implications need to be understood. Strict mode drops all ingress traffic if the best path back to the source is not the interface the traffic arrived on, so asymmetric routing will cause strict mode to drop legitimate traffic. Loose mode checks whether a route for the source exists at all, which may also discard legitimate traffic. The RFC expresses the hope that vendors will implement a DoS-mitigation mode in which the uRPF check fails only if the next hop for the source is a discard interface.

With uRPF enabled on interfaces at predetermined points in the network, and with the source addresses of attack traffic announced, the operator can drop the identified traffic at specified devices, ideally the ingress edge, based on the source address. Because the mechanism drops all traffic to and from that address, and not just the traffic to the victim, it is recommended that explicit policy be defined so that peers can only announce source-based RTBH routes for prefixes they originate.

The deployment steps are the same as for destination-based filtering, with one addition: uRPF is enabled on the chosen interfaces. The address or network to be blocked is announced using BGP tagged with a community, which installs the route with a next hop of the discard interface, so the uRPF check fails and the packets are discarded. The destination-based RTBH community must not be reused for source-based filtering, and the routes tagged with the chosen community must be carefully filtered. The BGP policy has to be relaxed to accept announcements carrying that community even though they contain addresses the announcing network does not control, and those announcements must not be propagated outside the local AS and should carry the NO_EXPORT community. As a matter of policy, operators should not accept source-based RTBH announcements from peers or customers; they should only be installed by local or attack management systems inside their own administrative domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Because attackers now follow the host name rather than the address, changing the address no longer helps. Black-holing the attacker's own address does help, but only if the router also checks that traffic really came from where it claims.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC is blunt about the risk: the techniques presented provide enough power to cause significant traffic forwarding loss if they are incorrectly deployed. It is imperative that the announcements that trigger the black holing are carefully checked, and that the BGP policy accepting those announcements is implemented so that the announcements are not propagated outside the AS, which is what the NO_EXPORT community is for; are not accepted from outside the AS, except from customers; and, except where source-based filtering is deployed, contain only networks that fall within the address ranges controlled by the announcing AS, so for a customer the address falls within that customer's own space.
sections.plainLanguage: These techniques can cut off a lot of traffic if they are set up wrongly, so the rules about who may trigger them and where the trigger may travel have to be enforced carefully.

sections.title: Sample Router Configurations
sections.content:
Two appendices give partial configurations, each with the warning that it is not complete and should be customised before use.

The Cisco sample has an announcing router and a filtering router. The announcing router holds the discard route as a static route to the null interface, an AS-path access list that matches an empty AS-PATH, and a route map that matches a tag of 666, sets the next hop to the discard address, sets a local preference of 200, adds the no-export community and the internal community 65505:666, and sets the origin to IGP. BGP then redistributes static routes through that route map. An example static route for 10.0.0.1 with the tag 666 means all traffic destined to that address is dropped. The filtering router repeats the discard route and the AS-path access list, and its route map matches a prefix list of host routes, the empty AS-PATH and the community 65505:666 with no-export, while denying anything else carrying that community. The interface that will do source-based filtering is configured with ip verify unicast source reachable-via any, which is loose mode.

The Juniper sample is the same idea in a different syntax. The announcing router has static routes for an example attack source and an example attack destination, both with the next hop 192.0.2.1 and the tag 666, and exports them to an internal BGP neighbour through a policy statement that sets the local preference, the origin, the community and the next hop, and accepts only /32 prefixes. The filtering router matches on the black-hole community, a local-only AS path and a /32 prefix length, sets no-export and the discard next hop, and enables unicast-reverse-path feasible-paths in the forwarding table, with the discard route as a static route.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendices show the same arrangement written for two vendors' routers, one announcing the trigger and one dropping the traffic.

sections.title: How the Technique Came About
sections.content:
The final appendix is a brief history of unicast RPF and RTBH filtering, contributed by Barry Raveendran Greene.

The loose check of uRPF was created by Neil Jarvis and Barry Greene as a rapid reaction tool for denial-of-service attacks, as a companion for destination-based RTBH. The requirement came out of conversations after the February 2000 attacks on several large content hosting companies, and was summarised as the Exodus Requirement: a tool to drop packets based on source IP address that can be pushed out to over 60 routers within 60 seconds, be longer than a thousand lines, be modified on the fly, and work in all platforms filtering at line rate.

Several options were considered, from reviving the Common Open Policy Service to pushing access control lists with BGP to creating a new protocol. In 2000 the quickest way to meet the requirement was to marry two functions. First, unicast RPF was modified so that the interface check was no longer required and a null or discard route would drop the packet, which is the loose check. Second, the technique of using BGP to trigger a distributed drop was revived and documented. Combining the two was judged a fast way to put a distributed packet-dropping capability into the industry's hands. The authors are clear that the loose check was created for this one purpose, and that its usefulness for other functions is a secondary benefit. It was not patented, and was published and disclosed in the document cited as Greene2001.
sections.plainLanguage: This started as an emergency measure after big hosting companies were flooded in February 2000. The requirement was to push a drop command to more than sixty routers within a minute, and the answer was to combine an existing routing check with the trick of announcing a route that goes nowhere.

viz.caption: THE FIVE SETUP STEPS FOR DESTINATION-BASED BLACK HOLING

items.title: 1. Discard addresses
items.text: Pick an address that means throw away, often from 192.0.2.0/24, and use a different one per incident.

items.title: 2. Discard route
items.text: Install a static route to the discard interface on the edge routers of the network.

items.title: 3. BGP policy
items.text: Match the chosen community and set the next hop to the discard address. Usually accept only /32s.

items.title: 4. Egress filters
items.text: Deny longer prefixes and the trigger communities on the way out, in case NO_EXPORT fails.

items.title: 5. Trigger router
items.text: A small device that sends the trigger over iBGP, carrying NO_EXPORT.
